title: Shake It Out: How Somatic Shaking Can Support Healing and Emotional Release
excerpt: What if one of the simplest ways to reconnect with your body was to simply shake it ? Shaking may look unusual at first, but trembling is a natural response to activation and stress.
author: Lia Natali

featuredImage.alt: Shake It Out: How Somatic Shaking Can Support Healing and Emotional Release

html:
What if one of the simplest ways to reconnect with your body was to simply shake it?

Shaking may look unusual at first, but trembling is a natural response to activation and stress. You may have experienced it yourself after a frightening situation, during intense nervousness, or after an emotionally overwhelming moment.

Animals also commonly shake after stressful experiences.

For humans, however, we often learn to suppress these natural physical responses. We hold ourselves still, tighten our muscles, control our breathing, and carry on with our day.

Somatic shaking offers another possibility: allowing the body to move, tremble, and release physical tension in a conscious and gentle way.

It is not about shaking as hard as possible. It is about becoming more aware of the body and allowing movement to happen without judgment.

What Is Somatic Shaking?

Somatic shaking is a body-based practice involving gentle shaking, trembling, bouncing, or rhythmic movement.

You can shake your hands and arms, gently bounce through your knees, move your shoulders and hips, or allow the movement to travel through your whole body.

There is no perfect technique.

The purpose is not to perform or look a certain way. Instead, you bring your attention into your body and notice what happens as you move.

Some people experience shaking as calming. Others feel more energised afterward. You might notice warmth, tingling, deeper breathing, emotional sensations, or simply a greater sense of being present in your body.

There doesn't have to be a dramatic experience for the practice to be beneficial.

The Connection Between Shaking and Stress

Stress isn't only something that happens in your mind.

Your body responds too.

Your shoulders may tighten. Your jaw may clench. Your breathing may become shallow. Your stomach may feel tense. You may feel restless, frozen, or unable to completely relax.

When stress continues for a long time, we can become accustomed to holding tension without even realising it.

Somatic shaking gives you an opportunity to bring movement into the body and become aware of these patterns.

Rather than telling yourself to "relax," you can use movement as a way of exploring what your body is actually experiencing.

Benefits of Shaking for Healing and Wellbeing

1. Helps Release Physical Tension

One of the most immediate reasons people enjoy shaking is the physical sensation.

Gentle shaking can bring movement into areas that feel tight or rigid, particularly the shoulders, arms, legs, hips, and back.

After several minutes, you may notice that your body feels warmer, looser, or more awake.

2. Supports Nervous System Regulation

Somatic shaking is often used as a nervous system regulation practice because it combines movement, body awareness, and rhythmic sensory input.

Instead of trying to force yourself to become calm, you give yourself an opportunity to notice activation and gradually shift your state.

The goal isn't to control your nervous system perfectly.

It is to become more familiar with how your body responds to stress—and how it feels when that activation begins to settle.

3. Creates Space for Emotional Release

Emotions have physical sensations.

Fear can make you tremble. Anger can create muscular tension. Anxiety can make you restless. Sadness can change the way you breathe.

Sometimes we become so accustomed to suppressing these sensations that we disconnect from them.

Shaking can provide a physical way to explore emotional activation without needing to analyse everything intellectually.

You might experience tears, laughter, a sigh, warmth, or nothing particularly emotional at all.

There is no emotion you need to produce.

The practice is simply an invitation to notice and allow.

4. Helps You Reconnect with Your Body

Many of us spend much of the day inside our heads—thinking, planning, working, worrying, and consuming information.

Somatic practices bring attention back to physical sensation.

While shaking, you might notice:

  • Where your body feels tense
  • Where you feel relaxed
  • How your breathing changes
  • Which movements feel comfortable
  • Where you tend to hold stress

Over time, this can develop greater body awareness and help you recognise your physical needs earlier.

5. Can Help Shift Mental Overload

When your mind is racing, trying to stop thinking can sometimes make you think even more.

Movement offers another doorway.

Instead of fighting your thoughts, you focus on your feet, your breathing, your muscles, and the sensation of movement.

For some people, this makes it easier to step out of repetitive thinking and become more present.

Is Shaking the Same as "Releasing Trauma"?

You may see somatic shaking described online as a way to "release trauma from the body."

It is important to approach this idea carefully.

Trauma is complex, and it cannot simply be shaken away. Shaking may be a useful body-awareness practice for some people, but it should not be presented as a replacement for trauma-informed professional care.

If a practice brings up intense memories, panic, dissociation, or overwhelming emotions, stop and seek appropriate support.

Healing doesn't require forcing a release.

Sometimes healing looks like moving. Sometimes it looks like resting. Sometimes it means getting professional support. And sometimes it simply means learning to feel safe enough to listen to your body.

How to Practise Gentle Somatic Shaking

You can try shaking for just 2–5 minutes.

Stand comfortably with your feet about hip-width apart and keep your knees soft.

Begin by gently shaking your hands.

Allow the movement to travel into your arms and shoulders. Then gradually include your knees, hips, and legs.

Let your body move naturally rather than trying to create a particular shape or rhythm.

Keep your breathing comfortable.

After a few minutes, gradually reduce the movement until you become still.

Then pause.

Notice your feet on the ground. Notice your breathing. Notice how your body feels compared with when you started.

You don't need to experience a huge emotional release.

The practice is about awareness, not performance.

Shaking Can Be Part of a Larger Healing Practice

Somatic shaking doesn't have to exist on its own.

It can be combined with other forms of mindful movement such as Qigong, yoga, breathwork, gentle dance, or meditation.

These practices can help you explore different aspects of the mind-body connection: grounding, breath, movement, awareness, relaxation, and presence.

The more you listen to your body, the more you may begin to recognise what it is asking for.

Sometimes it wants movement.

Sometimes it wants stillness.

Sometimes it simply wants you to stop and pay attention.

Let Your Body Move

You don't always have to think your way through stress.

Sometimes, the body needs a different language.

A few minutes of gentle shaking can be a simple way to move out of physical rigidity, reconnect with sensation, and create more space for awareness.

You don't have to shake perfectly. You don't have to force an emotional release. You simply begin—and listen.

Because healing is not always about doing more. Sometimes, it begins with giving your body permission to move, feel, and come back to itself.
